specs.name: Photo Library Search (AI descriptions)
specs.tagline: Let your AI search thousands of your own photos by what is in them — a receipt, your passport, the whiteboard from that meeting — without uploading your library.
keywords: find a photo on my computer

actions.label: Describe my photos (build the search index)
actions.description: Looks at every photo in a folder (and its subfolders) with a small AI model that runs on your computer, and writes one line per photo — what's in it, any readable text, the date — into an index file. Run it again any time: photos already in the index are skipped, so it picks up where it left off. Works offline — everything it needs is included in the app. Photos are never uploaded.
actions.mcpDescription: Build or extend a searchable index of a photo folder on the user's computer, offline: a small vision model (SmolVLM-500M via llama.cpp) writes a one-to-two-sentence description of each image (kind of image, subjects, place, readable text), saved as `path<TAB>date<TAB>description` lines in `out`. Photos already in that index are skipped, so call it repeatedly with the same `folder` and `out` to work through a big library `limit` photos at a time (a few seconds per photo); the result says how many are left. Formats: JPG, PNG, WebP, TIFF, BMP, GIF, and HEIC/HEIF (iPhone) on macOS. Then use photos_search to find photos ('my passport', 'receipt from the hardware store', 'whiteboard', 'dog on the beach'), or read the index yourself. Nothing is uploaded or changed. Descriptions come from a small model and can be wrong in details (it may misread or invent text, numbers or dates): before relying on a detail, look at the photo itself.

argv: Describe what is visible in this image in one or two plain sentences: the kind of image (photo, screenshot, document, receipt, ID card, whiteboard, drawing...), the main subjects and the setting. Then copy up to 15 words of clearly readable text exactly. Never guess names, numbers or dates you cannot read.

actions.successMessage: Photos described and added to the index.

actions.label: Describe my videos (add them to the search index)
actions.description: Adds the videos in a folder (and its subfolders) to the same search index as your photos: nine frames from the start of each video are shown to the AI model on your computer, which writes what the video shows. Already-indexed videos are skipped. Nothing is uploaded.
actions.mcpDescription: Add the videos in a folder on the user's computer to a photo search index (same `out` file as photos_index), offline: 9 frames from each video's first ~45 seconds are put in a contact sheet and a small vision model (SmolVLM-500M via llama.cpp) describes what the video shows, saved as `path<TAB>date<TAB>description`. Already-indexed videos are skipped; call again to continue (`limit` per run, the result says how many are left). Formats: MP4, MOV, M4V, MKV, AVI, WEBM. Then use photos_search to find a video ('the kids at the beach', 'birthday cake', 'screen recording of the settings page'). For what is said in a video, use transcribe/watch tools. Descriptions come from a small model and can be wrong in details (it may misread or invent text, numbers or dates): before relying on a detail, look at the photo itself.

argv: These are 9 frames from one video, in order, in a 3 by 3 grid. In one or two plain sentences, describe what is visible in the video: the setting, the main subjects and what happens. Never guess names, numbers or dates. Do not mention the grid.

actions.successMessage: Videos described and added to the index.

actions.label: Search my photos
actions.description: Type what you're looking for — "passport", "receipt", "whiteboard", "dog on the beach" — and get the best-matching photos from your index, with their dates and descriptions.
actions.mcpDescription: Search a photo index made by photos_index for photos matching a description (words are matched against each photo's AI description, date and file path; best matches first). Returns `path<TAB>date<TAB>description` lines. Use for 'find the photo of my passport / that receipt / the whiteboard from the March meeting / pictures of the dog at the beach'. If nothing matches, try different words (what would be visible in the picture). You can also read the index file directly for complex questions. Descriptions can be wrong in details — open the matching photo to confirm before telling the user it is the one.

actions.mcpDescription: Turn text into natural-sounding English speech and save it as a .wav audio file on the user's computer, offline (Kokoro voices; no account, no cloud). Use this whenever the user wants a voiceover, narration, podcast intro, audiobook chapter, announcement, or wants a document/notes read aloud or 'saved as audio'. Write or clean up the script first, then pass it as `text` (up to ~20,000 characters per call; split longer documents into chapters and call once per chapter). Pick `voice` to match the request (US/UK, female/male).

actions.label: Who spoke when
actions.description: Pick a meeting, interview or podcast recording. You get a timeline of who is speaking when (Speaker 1, Speaker 2, …). Combine it with a transcript to see who said what.
actions.mcpDescription: Detect who is speaking when in an audio or video recording on the user's computer (speaker diarization, offline): returns lines like '[00:01:05 → 00:01:20] Speaker 2'. Use for meetings, interviews, podcasts and calls when the user wants speaker labels or 'who said what' — run transcribe_transcribe with timestamps as well and match the times to label each line of the transcript with its speaker. Set `speakers` if the number of people is known.

actions.mcpDescription: Transcribe an audio or video file on the user's computer (mp3, m4a, wav, mp4, mov, …) to text with Whisper, offline. Returns the full transcript (optionally with [hh:mm:ss] timestamps) and can also save it to a .txt file (`out`). Set `translate` to get an English translation instead. Use this whenever the user wants a recording, voice memo, meeting or video turned into text, notes or a summary.

actions.label: Meeting transcript (who said what)
actions.description: For meetings, interviews and podcasts: a transcript where every line says who is speaking (Speaker 1, Speaker 2, …) with timestamps. Works offline — the models are included in the app.
actions.mcpDescription: Transcribe a meeting, interview, call or podcast recording on the user's computer into a speaker-labelled transcript ('[00:01:05] Speaker 2: …'), offline: Whisper speech-to-text plus speaker diarization in one step. Use whenever the user wants meeting notes, minutes, action items per person, an interview transcript, or 'who said what'. Afterwards you can rename 'Speaker 1/2' to real names if the user tells you who is who, and summarize.

actions.mcpDescription: Create subtitles/captions (.srt) for a video or audio file on the user's computer with Whisper, offline: speech is transcribed and timed into readable captions, in the spoken language or translated to English (`translate`). Use whenever the user wants subtitles, captions or an .srt for a video (YouTube, TikTok, Reels, lectures, accessibility). To put them into the video afterwards, call ffmpeg_add_subtitles.

actions.label: Make a narrated video
actions.description: Pick your photos (in order), type or paste the script, choose a voice. You get an MP4: your photos in turn, the script read aloud by a natural AI voice, and captions timed to the speech. The photos loop until the narration ends. actions.mcpDescription: Make a narrated video (MP4) on the user's computer, offline: the given photos/images are shown in order (each for `seconds`, looping until the narration ends), the `script` is read aloud by a natural AI voice (Kokoro, US/UK English) and captions timed to the speech are burned in (Whisper). Use whenever the user wants a video from photos with a voiceover — product promos, real-estate tours, recaps, explainers, social posts, slideshows with narration. Write the script yourself if the user only describes what they want (about 150 words per minute of video). Pick `size` for where it will be posted (landscape for YouTube, portrait for Reels/TikTok/Shorts, square for feeds).

actions.description: Pick a song or video. You get two files: the music without vocals (instrumental / karaoke) and the vocals on their own. Works offline — everything it needs is included in the app.
actions.mcpDescription: Separate a song (any audio or video file on the user's computer) into an instrumental/karaoke track with the vocals removed and a vocals-only (acapella) track, offline with the UVR MDX-Net model. specs.name: Video to Screenshots & Transcript
specs.tagline: Turn a video into timed screenshots and a timestamped transcript — so you (or your AI) can see and read what happens in it.

upstream.license: GPL (FFmpeg static build), Apache-2.0/MIT (Whisper via sherpa-onnx)

actions.label: Screenshots + transcript
actions.description: Pick a video and a folder. You get a screenshot every few seconds (frame_0001.jpg is the start, then one every interval) and transcript.txt with what is said and when. Great for writing a how-to from a screen recording, notes from a lecture, or finding a moment in a long video. Silent videos work too (screenshots only).
actions.mcpDescription: Let the AI 'watch' a video on the user's computer, offline: saves a screenshot every `every` seconds into `outDir` (frame_0001.jpg = 0:00, frame_0002.jpg = `every` seconds later, and so on; at most 300) plus transcript.txt with timestamped speech ([hh:mm:ss] lines, Whisper). Then open the screenshots and the transcript yourself to answer questions about the video, summarise it, write step-by-step docs or a tutorial from a screen recording, find when something is shown or said, or pick timestamps for clips. Use `every` 2 for fast screen recordings, 5 for normal videos, 15-30 for long lectures or meetings. Silent videos are fine (the transcript then says no speech was found).

prepare.emptyText: (No speech was found in this video.)

actions.successMessage: Screenshots and transcript.txt saved in the folder.

actions.label: Watch my screen (record + explain)
actions.description: Records your screen — and your voice, if a microphone is available — for the time you choose, so you can show your AI something instead of describing it: a bug, a task you do every week, how a program works. You get a screenshot each time the screen changes (named by the second it happened) plus a timestamped transcript of what you said. On a Mac, allow Screen Recording (and Microphone) for the app that runs this, the first time.
actions.mcpDescription: Watch the user's screen live: records the screen (and microphone, when available) for `seconds`, while the user shows you something and explains it out loud — reproducing a bug, a task to automate, how an app is used. Saves into `outDir`: frame_<N>.jpg each time the screen changes (N = tenths of a second from the start, so frame_123.jpg = 12.3 s; only changed screens, at most 300), transcript.txt with [hh:mm:ss] lines of what the user said, and recording.mp4. BEFORE calling, tell the user: 'Recording your screen for N seconds starts now — show me and talk me through it.' Afterwards open transcript.txt and the frames to understand what happened. macOS needs Screen Recording (and Microphone) permission for the app that runs the MCP server; Linux needs an X11 session (not Wayland).

options.label: Yes — I'll explain while I show

prepare.emptyText: (Nothing was said during the recording, or no microphone was available.)

actions.successMessage: Recording saved — screenshots of every change and a transcript.

actions.label: Look through my webcam
actions.description: Takes a photo with your computer's camera after a short countdown, so your AI can see something physical: a part you're holding up, a whiteboard, a handwritten note, a plant, a 3D print in progress. Nothing is uploaded by this app; the photo is saved where you choose.
actions.mcpDescription: Take a photo with the user's webcam and return it to you as an image, so you can see something physical: an object or part the user holds up, a whiteboard, handwriting, a label, a device's lights or screen, a 3D print or plant to check on. `wait` is the countdown in seconds before the photo (gives the camera time to adjust and the user time to position things — ask them to hold the object close and steady). Call it again whenever you need another look; for monitoring something over time, call it on an interval. Use only when the user asks you to look; the photo is saved to `out` on their computer. If no camera is found, ask the user to connect one and allow camera access for GUI Hub (macOS: System Settings → Privacy & Security → Camera).
